steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The residents of Sierra should vote in favor of a local tax to fund construction of the proposed road.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
The builders won't finish the Glen Veil complex unless a road connecting it to Sierra is built. So the road is required for the complex.

If the complex is completed, it will strengthen Sierra's economy, and a stronger economy would benefit every Sierra resident.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Line up what the premises give us against what the conclusion asks for.

The premises are all about benefit. The complex is waiting on the road, the finished complex strengthens the economy, and the stronger economy helps every resident.

The conclusion is about duty: residents should vote for a tax. Nothing in the premises says that benefiting from something means you ought to vote to fund it. That's the new idea the conclusion brings in, and it's the gap.

There's also a cost the developer never weighs. A tax costs every resident something too. The developer simply treats the benefit as enough to settle the vote. A principle that justifies this reasoning has to make that move for us.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
On a justify-the-reasoning principle, the answer usually has the shape If Evidence, then Conclusion, written in general terms. Here the evidence boils down to benefit, and the conclusion is a vote for a tax. So predict:

would benefit from a construction project → should vote for a tax that funds it

The right side has to say residents should vote in favor. A principle that only tells us when not to vote for a tax, or who should pay one, can't deliver that conclusion.

notes.body: A fires only when a project is "necessary in order to strengthen a town’s economy". The road is necessary for the complex, but nothing says the complex is the only way to strengthen Sierra's economy, so we can't show the road is necessary for a stronger economy. The trigger isn't established, and A never touches the benefit to every resident that the developer argues from.

This is the tempting one, because it talks about results that "benefit all of those residents", which is exactly what the developer established. But read the direction. B says residents "should not vote in favor" of the tax unless everyone benefits. That makes benefit to all a requirement for a yes vote:

a yes vote is acceptable → the project benefits all residents

The developer has the right side, not the left. Meeting a requirement only keeps a yes vote from being ruled out. It never tells residents they should vote yes, and that is the conclusion we need.

C only applies once a town is funding a project, and then it compares a tax with debt. The developer's question is whether residents should back this tax at all. C never mentions benefit, so the developer's evidence can't trigger it, and its outcome is about the form of funding, not about how residents should vote.

D is about who "should be required to pay" a tax. The developer's conclusion is about how residents should vote, not who gets billed. And D only limits payment to beneficiaries. Knowing everyone benefits makes everyone eligible to pay, but being eligible to pay is not a reason anyone should vote for the tax.

E is the If Evidence, then Conclusion principle we predicted. Its left side, anyone "who would benefit from the results of a construction project", matches the developer's evidence: the road is required for the complex to be finished, and the complex strengthens the economy and benefits every Sierra resident. Its right side, "should vote in favor of a local tax to fund that project", is the conclusion almost word for word.

The move to repeat: when the conclusion says someone should do something and the premises only describe facts, look for the principle whose left side is built from the premises and whose right side is the should. E supplies the missing bridge from benefit to duty.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: The residents of Sierra should vote in favor of a local tax to fund construction of the proposed road.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body:
If the proposed road connecting GVAC to Sierra isn't built, then the builders of GVAC won't complete the complex.
Were the complex to be completed, it would strengthen Sierra's economy and that would benefit every Sierra resident.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
Why does the author think that residents of Sierra should vote in favor of a tax that would fund this proposed road? Ultimately, the author says, because it would benefit every Sierra resident (by making the economy stronger).
Naturally, increasing local taxes would also affect every Sierra resident, so there's an element of weighing tradeoffs going into this recommendation: you should vote to have a new tax imposed because the benefit you'll ultimately get from the stronger economy is worth it?

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body:
It's hard to predict what ideas they'll pair up in the correct answer choice.
When it comes to Premise facts, we know the proposed road
- is required to complete construction of something that, if constructed, would strengthen the economy / benefit everyone
When it comes to what the Conclusion wants to hear, it's ideas like
- this is a good tax to vote for
- we do want this apartment complex to be completed
- the benefit of the stronger economy would outweigh the harm of the new tax.

old_notes.body: This principle requires the project to be "necessary" for economic growth. The developer only claims the apartment complex would strengthen the economy, not that it is the only way to do so. The mismatch is between sufficiency and necessity. The developer argues the project is sufficient to produce benefits, but this principle demands that it be necessary — indispensable. Since other projects could also strengthen the economy, the developer cannot meet this principle's trigger condition. A principle requiring only that a project would benefit residents, rather than that it is indispensable, would be a better fit.

This principle states that residents should not vote for a tax increase unless the resulting benefits accrue to all residents. While the developer does claim the economy strengthening would benefit every resident, this principle is structured as a negative condition — a reason to vote no if the condition is not met, rather than a positive reason to vote yes when it is. More importantly, this principle could easily be weaponized against the developer: any resident who argues they would not personally benefit could use this principle to justify opposition. The developer needs a principle that positively connects benefit to voting obligation, not one that sets a high bar that could defeat the proposal.

This principle addresses whether projects should be funded by taxes versus debt — the method of financing. The developer's logical gap is not about which funding mechanism is best but about why residents should support this particular expenditure at all. A principle about taxation being preferable to borrowing does not bridge the gap between "you would benefit" and "you should vote for the tax." Even if taxes are the ideal funding method, this says nothing about why residents should approve this specific tax for this specific project. The principle operates in the wrong analytical domain entirely.

This principle states that only those who benefit from a project should be required to pay for it. At first glance, this seems supportive — the developer claims residents benefit, so they should pay. But the principle creates a dangerous counter-argument. The developer wants all residents to vote yes. This principle implies that residents who do NOT benefit should NOT pay the tax. Any resident could argue "I will not personally benefit from apartments I will not live in," and this principle would support their opposition. Rather than unifying residents behind the tax, it fragments them into beneficiaries who should pay and non-beneficiaries who should not — undermining the developer's blanket appeal.

This principle precisely fills the gap in the developer's argument. The developer establishes that residents would benefit from the project. This principle states that anyone who would benefit from a project should vote for the tax that funds it. Applied together: (1) the road enables an apartment complex that strengthens the economy (premise), (2) a stronger economy benefits every resident (premise), (3) anyone who benefits should vote for the funding tax (this principle), (4) therefore, residents should vote for the tax increase (conclusion). Without this principle, there is no logical reason why benefiting from something obligates you to support its funding. This principle provides that normative bridge, making the conclusion follow necessarily from the premises.

steps.label: Main Conclusion
steps.body: We should not be persuaded by Graham's argument.

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: People sleep, and at least sometimes when sleeping they are truly happy, even though they are not doing anything.

steps.label: Opposing Point (Graham's conclusion)
steps.body: The best life is a life that is full of activity.

steps.label: Opposing Point (Graham's premise)
steps.body: A person is truly happy only when doing something.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Two arguments are stacked here. Graham's: a person is truly happy only when doing something, so the best life is full of activity. The philosopher's: we shouldn't be persuaded by Graham's argument, because people are sometimes truly happy while sleeping, when they aren't doing anything.

Which part of Graham's argument does the sleep claim hit? Graham's premise is a conditional:

truly happy → doing something

A sleeper who is truly happy while doing nothing has the left side without the right side. That's a counterexample to the premise.

Notice what the philosopher does not claim. The philosopher never says the best life isn't full of activity. The conclusion is only that Graham's argument shouldn't persuade us. Knocking out a premise is enough for that, because an argument with a false premise doesn't establish its conclusion, even if the conclusion happens to be true.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The claim in the stem is the philosopher's premise, and its job is to show that Graham's premise is false. Look for an answer that names both pieces: an example, aimed at Graham's premise rather than Graham's conclusion.

notes.body: A gets the owner wrong. Graham's premise is that a person is truly happy only when doing something. The sleep claim contradicts that, so it can't be part of Graham's argument. It belongs to the philosopher, who uses it against Graham.

B names both the form and the target. It is an example: a sleeper who is truly happy while doing nothing is one specific case. And it aims to show that "a premise of Graham’s argument is false": the case breaks Graham's premise that true happiness requires doing something.

The move to repeat on Role questions: when a speaker attacks someone else's argument, ask which part the attack lands on, the premise or the conclusion. Then match the answer to that exact target.

Graham never mentions sleep. The sleeping case is the philosopher's own, and the philosopher relies on it rather than rejecting it. It isn't an analogy either: it is a direct case of happiness without activity, not a comparison to some other situation.

D is the closest trap, because the claim is an example and it is aimed at Graham. But it hits the premise, not the conclusion. A happy sleeper doesn't show that the best life isn't full of activity; a busy life could still be best for other reasons. That's why the philosopher concludes only that we shouldn't be persuaded, not that Graham's conclusion is false.

The main conclusion is that we should not be persuaded by Graham's argument. Ask why we should believe that. Because people are sometimes truly happy while sleeping. The sleep claim answers the why, so it is support for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.

old_steps.label: Main Conclusion
old_steps.body: We should not be persuaded by Graham's argument

old_steps.label: Premise
old_steps.body: People sleep, and at least sometimes when sleeping they are truly happy, even though they are not doing anything.

old_steps.label: Opposing Point
old_steps.body: The best life is a life that is full of activity.

old_steps.label: Opposing Point
old_steps.body: A person is truly happy only when doing something.

old_notes.body: The claim is a premise of the philosopher’s argument and not of Graham’s argument.
This correctly describes the role and purpose of the claim.
Graham never appeals to sleep; the sleeping example is the philosopher's own. And the philosopher does not reject it, but relies on it to show that one of Graham's premises is false.
While the claim is an example, it is not intended to disprove Graham’s conclusion, but rather a premise of Graham’s argument.
The claim is not the main conclusion of the philosopher’s argument but rather a premise.

steps.label: Conclusion (it follows that)
steps.body: The sole reason that sexual reproduction has become the rule among both animals and plants is that natural selection has favored some entire species over others.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction is that it increases the range of genetic variation in a species, which is an advantage for the species as a whole. However, an increased range of genetic variation in a species is not advantageous for any individual member of the species.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
"It follows that" marks the last sentence as the conclusion: the sole reason sexual reproduction became the rule is that natural selection favored some entire species over others.

Why should we believe it? The biologist gives two facts that work together. First, the advantage of sexual reproduction is wider genetic variation, which helps the species as a whole. Second, that variation helps no individual member. If the advantage shows up only at the species level, selection among individuals can't explain why sexual reproduction spread. That leaves selection among whole species, which is the conclusion.

Slow down on the "However". It contrasts species with individuals, but it doesn't turn against the biologist. Both sentences are on the conclusion's side. The second one actually does the heavier lifting, since it is what rules out an individual-level explanation.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The stem asks about the second premise, the claim that the variation helps no individual. Predict: a premise that supports the conclusion. Expect an answer as plain as a claim offered in support of the conclusion.

notes.body:
That's the prediction. The claim about individuals is offered as a reason, and the conclusion depends on it: once individuals gain nothing from the variation, the remaining explanation is selection among whole species.

The move to repeat: find the conclusion by its indicator, then ask of the target claim whether it answers why we should believe the conclusion. If it does, it is support, no matter what contrast word introduces it.

B reads the "However" as a turn against the conclusion. The turn is between two premises: good for the species, but not for individuals. Test it: if individuals did benefit, the conclusion would get weaker, because individual selection could then explain the spread. So the claim helps the conclusion. It doesn't cast doubt on it.

The argument never questions this claim. It asserts it and builds on it. A claim the argument is designed to call into question would be something the biologist argues against, and the biologist argues from this one.

The phenomenon the biologist explains is that sexual reproduction "has become the rule among both animals and plants". The target claim isn't that phenomenon. It is a fact about who benefits from genetic variation, used to help explain the spread.

The explanation the argument offers is in the conclusion: natural selection favoring some entire species over others. The target claim helps rule out the rival, individual-level explanation, which is why the species-level one wins. Helping to establish an explanation is not the same as being the explanation.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (it follows that)
old_steps.body: The sole reason that sexual reproduction has become the rule among both animals and plants is that natural selection has favored some entire species over others.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: The evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction is that it increases the range of genetic variation in a species, which is an advantage for the species as a whole. But an increased range of genetic variation in a species is not advantageous for any individual member of the species.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The word "however" in the second sentence indicates a pivot from the idea in the first sentence to a different, contrasting idea. In the final sentence, the phrase "it follows that" indicates that this final sentence contains a conclusion, supported by evidence in the previous sentences.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: The statement quoted by the question stem is in the second sentence of the stimulus, which contains the argument's evidence or premise.

old_notes.body: The quoted statement is evidence — a claim that supports the conclusion. It establishes that genetic variation does not benefit individuals, which forces the explanation for sexual reproduction's prevalence to the species level. This directly supports the conclusion about species-level natural selection.

The quoted statement does not raise doubt about the conclusion — it supports it. By showing that genetic variation does not benefit individuals, it strengthens the case for species-level selection. It is an ally of the conclusion, not a challenger.
The argument does not call the quoted statement into question — it embraces it as support for the conclusion. The argument builds upon this claim rather than attempting to undermine it.

The conclusion explains why sexual reproduction has become the rule — the "observed phenomenon" if there is one. But the quoted statement is about whether genetic variation benefits individuals, which is evidence, not the phenomenon being explained. The phenomenon the argument seeks to explain is the prevalence of sexual reproduction, described in the conclusion itself.

The main explanation of why sexual reproduction prevails is in the conclusion: species-level natural selection. The quoted statement is not the explanation — it is evidence that leads to the explanation. It establishes that individual-level selection cannot explain sexual reproduction, which then supports the species-level explanation in the conclusion.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Emotion is not nonrational.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: Emotion only seems nonrational because language lacks the ability to convey adequate conceptions of emotion.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
The words we use to refer to emotions name only very general kinds of inner experience, such as excitement, calm and joy.

Illustration of that: there is no language for describing just how one joy differs from another.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Role and Main Conclusion arguments often put the conclusion right after a pivot that pushes back on someone's view. Here the philosopher opens with how philosophers usually treat emotions, as nonrational, then pivots with "But": emotion is not nonrational. That's the main conclusion.

Everything after it is support, in layers. Why believe emotion isn't nonrational? Because it only seems that way, since language can't convey adequate conceptions of emotion. Why believe language falls short? Because emotion words name only very general kinds of experience.

Then the last sentence opens with "Thus, for example". Two signals that seem to fight. "Thus" usually marks something that follows; "for example" marks an illustration. Both fit. If emotion words are only general, they can't separate one joy from another, so the last sentence follows from the general claim. And it is offered as one concrete case of that general claim. It isn't where the argument is headed. It is a picture of the evidence.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The target claim is a specific case of the general claim about emotion words, and that general claim supports the main conclusion through the middle step about language. Predict an answer that calls it an example or illustration of a supporting claim, with only an indirect link to the main conclusion.

notes.body: The phenomenon the argument explains is that emotion seems nonrational. An example of that would be a case of someone treating an emotion as nonrational. The joy claim is nothing like that. It is a case of language being too general, which is part of the explanation, not part of what gets explained.

The main conclusion is "emotion is not nonrational", right after the "But". The joy claim is offered to help support it, so it can't be it. "Thus" is the bait. Here it shows the joy claim follows from the general point about emotion words, and "for example" shows it illustrates that point. A main conclusion is where the argument ends up, and this sentence is a step on the way.

C traces the support chain exactly. One joy versus another is "a specific instance", a single case. It is "illustrating a general claim," the claim that emotion words name only very general kinds of experience. And it is "thereby indirectly supporting the conclusion", because that general claim backs the point about language, which backs the conclusion that emotion isn't nonrational.

The move to repeat: when a role answer says indirectly, check that a middle claim sits between the target and the conclusion. Here one does, so indirectly is accurate.

A concession grants something to the other side. The other side says emotion is nonrational. The joy claim grants nothing to that view. It supports the philosopher's account of why emotion only seems nonrational, so it works against the opposing view.

E is tempting because the joy claim sits close to the explanation. But the explanation offered for why emotion seems nonrational is that "language lacks the ability to convey adequate conceptions of emotion." The joy claim is one case under the general point about emotion words, which in turn backs that explanation. It illustrates the support. It isn't the explanation itself.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Emotion is not nonrational.

old_steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
old_steps.body: Emotion only seems nonrational way because language lacks the ability to convey adequate conceptions of emotion.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: The words we use to refer to emotions name only very general kinds of inner experience, such as excitement / calm / joy, but there is no language for describing just how one joy differs from another.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: Whenever we do Main Conclusion / Role, we listen for Rebuttal/Pivot conclusions (most of them are that style) or First Sentence conclusions (the 2nd most common style). Since this paragraph begins with an Attribution, "Philosophers usually think of emotions as X", we'd be waiting for a Pivot + Pushback, and so when we see "But emotion is not nonrational", we most likely have our rebuttal conclusion. Everything after that is support for the main conclusion. They're asking us about the last sentence, which is hella confusing because it's prefaced by Thus (which usually indicates conclusion) and by "for example" (which always indicates support). How can the last claim be a conclusion and a premise?! We need to remember that premise/conclusion indicator words can also be used to indicate Cause/Effect. "Since I have the flu, I have a fever." / "I have the flu. Thus, I have a fever." That's why we see a Thus in front of this supporting idea. The previous sentence causes this last claim to be true. The fact that we have words for only general emotional states is why we don't have specific words for different types of joy.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: We know this final claim plays a supporting role, and we know that the main conclusion is "Emotion is not nonrational", that's good enough to head to the answers.

old_notes.body: When it comes to the main conclusion, the argument does not seek to explain a phenomenon. It seeks to oppose the idea that emotions are nonrational. Emotions are a phenomenon, but the author isn't trying to explain why emotions happen. She's just trying to classify them as rational or nonrational. (To explain a phenomenon means to provide a causal explanation for it) Within the subsidiary argument, the author is trying to provide a causal explanation for the phenomenon of why people think emotions are nonrational. But an example of that phenomenon would be a specific case where a person thought of an emotion as nonrational. The last sentence doesn't resemble that at all, so even if we were being charitable to this answer, it breaks down.

The main conclusion is that emotion is not nonrational. The target statement — about one joy being indistinguishable from another in language — is evidence supporting the general claim about language's limitations, which in turn supports the conclusion. The word "thus" before this statement might suggest it is a conclusion, but "for example" immediately overrides that signal, identifying the statement as an illustration. The conclusion appears earlier in the argument, not at the end.

The target statement illustrates a specific instance of the general claim that emotion-words name only very general kinds of experience. "Joy" is a general word, and there is no language to capture how one joy differs from another — that is a specific example of language's generality. This general claim about language, in turn, supports the conclusion that emotion is not nonrational but merely appears so because of linguistic limitations. The target statement thus indirectly supports the conclusion by illustrating the evidence that directly supports it.

A concession would acknowledge the opposing view's validity. The opposing view is that emotions are nonrational. The target statement — about language's inability to distinguish joys — does not concede that emotions are nonrational. Instead, it supports the argument's rebuttal of that view by showing that language is inadequate, which is why emotions merely appear nonrational. The target statement works against the opposing view, not in its favor.

The explanation proposed for why emotions seem nonrational is that "language lacks the ability to convey adequate conceptions of emotion." That appears in the second sentence. The target statement — about one joy being indistinguishable from another — is an example illustrating that explanation, not the explanation itself. This answer confuses the general explanation with the specific illustration. The explanation is the broad claim about language; the target statement is one piece of supporting evidence for that claim.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: For early humans who moved from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to agriculture, the transition must have been traumatic.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: There would have been increased incidence of disease and injury and a more homogeneous diet lacking vital nutrients more easily obtainable from the richly varied diet of hunter-gatherers.

steps.label: Main Conclusion
steps.body: Groups that made the transition were likely motivated by certain benefits that accompany the settled life of the agriculturist, such as opportunities for the accumulation of wealth by those with specialized social roles.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with the indicator. "Thus" opens the last sentence, so that's a conclusion: groups that switched to agriculture were likely motivated by benefits of settled life.

Now test the first sentence the way we test any candidate: why should we believe the transition was traumatic? The second sentence answers. More disease and injury, and a diet lacking vital nutrients. So the first sentence has support of its own.

Does it support anything? Yes. Why think the groups were drawn by benefits like wealth? Because the switch was traumatic, and the argument's thought is that groups wouldn't accept that kind of hardship without something to gain. So the traumatic claim is supported by the second sentence and supports the last one. That makes it an intermediate conclusion.

The first sentence looks like a classic first-sentence conclusion. It is a conclusion, just not the main one. "Thus" settles which one is main.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The quoted claim is an intermediate conclusion, but the answer may not use that phrase. It might call the claim a premise that has support of its own. Look for an answer that says the claim is supported and also supports the main conclusion.

notes.body:
Here is the intermediate conclusion in disguise. The claim is "a premise" because it supports the main conclusion, and "another premise is offered as support" because the disease, injury and diet sentence backs it up.

The move to repeat: on Role questions, run two checks on the target claim. Does something support it? Does it support something? Two yeses means an intermediate conclusion, whatever words the answer uses for it.

B says the claim "plays no logical role". Remove it and see what happens. The second sentence would be left with nothing to prove, and the conclusion would lose the hardship that makes the benefits worth mentioning. A claim that holds the argument together is not background.

C is the trap for anyone who stopped after the first sentence. It gets half right: the claim does act as a premise for the conclusion. The failure is the second half. Ask why we should believe the transition was traumatic. The very next sentence answers: more disease and injury, and a diet lacking vital nutrients. That is support, so "no support is offered" is false.

The conclusion of the argument as a whole comes after "Thus": groups that switched were likely motivated by the benefits of settled life. The traumatic claim is a step toward that point. It is a conclusion, but only an intermediate one.

Nothing in the argument pushes back on the traumatic claim. The anthropologist supports it with evidence and then builds on it. A claim the argument seeks to rebut would be followed by reasons it is wrong, and here every reason points the other way.

old_steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
old_steps.body: For early humans who moved from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to agriculture, the transition must have been traumatic.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: There would have been increased incidence of disease and injury and a more homogeneous diet lacking vital nutrients more easily obtainable from the richly varied diet of hunter-gatherers.

old_steps.label: Main Conclusion
old_steps.body: Groups that made the transition were likely motivated by certain benefits that accompany the settled life of the agriculturist, such as opportunities for the accumulation of wealth by those with specialized social roles.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The statement that is quoted in the question stem is an intermediate conclusion. It is supported by the evidence in the second sentence, and supports the main conclusion in the final sentence.

old_notes.body: The quoted statement supports the main conclusion and is itself supported by another premise (disease, injury, diet evidence). The LSAT's description — "a premise for which another premise is offered as support" — accurately captures both relationships. While we might call this an "intermediate conclusion," calling it a "premise" is not technically wrong since it does support the main conclusion.

The statement plays a direct logical role — it supports the main conclusion and is supported by evidence. Background information would be a neutral fact that sets the scene without participating in the argument's logic.

This claims no support is offered for the quoted statement. But the second sentence — increased disease, injury, and a less nutritious diet — directly supports the claim that the transition was traumatic. Support is clearly offered.
The main conclusion is the final sentence, introduced by "thus." The quoted statement supports this conclusion but is not the conclusion itself.

The argument supports and builds upon the "traumatic" claim rather than seeking to rebut it. An opposing viewpoint would be contested by the argument, but this statement is firmly integrated into the argument's reasoning.

steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
steps.body: A successful legal system prohibits only those few behaviors that citizens find absolutely intolerable.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The purpose of laws in a legal system is to deter bad actions by threatening punishment if you perform them, but this only works if people think they're likely to get punished for committing those actions, and the more behaviors that are criminalized, the less likely someone will be caught and punished.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Role and Main Conclusion, it pays to check the first sentence and any pivot before trusting the end. Here neither holds up. The first sentence, about the purpose of a law, gets no support from anything else. The "But" sentence, about the odds of being caught dropping as prohibitions multiply, isn't supported either. A claim with no support can't be a conclusion.

That leaves the "Therefore" sentence, and this time it really is the main conclusion: a successful legal system prohibits only the few behaviors citizens find absolutely intolerable. Why believe that? Laws work by threatening punishment. The threat works only if people think they're likely to be punished. And the more kinds of acts are prohibited, the less likely punishment becomes. Keep the list short, and the threat stays believable.

The first sentence is the starting point of that chain. Nothing supports it, and it supports the conclusion.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The target is the first sentence. It supports the conclusion and has no support of its own. Predict: a premise.

notes.body: A invents a conclusion. The scholar never mentions police officers or how many a legal system needs. The stated conclusion is about limiting the number of prohibited behaviors, and the first sentence supports that. An answer built on a conclusion the argument never draws can't describe a role in it.

The conclusion comes after "Therefore": a successful legal system prohibits only a few intolerable behaviors. Ask whether anything supports the first sentence. Nothing does. It is a starting point, and a claim with nothing behind it can't be the conclusion.

C matches the prediction. The first sentence starts the chain: laws deter through threatened punishment, the threat needs believable punishment, more prohibitions make punishment less likely, so prohibit only the intolerable. Nothing earlier props it up.

The move to repeat: two questions settle most Role answers. Is the claim supported? Does it support something? Here the answers are no and yes. That combination is a plain premise.

D is the trap for students who expect Role questions to ask about an intermediate conclusion. An intermediate conclusion has both jobs: it gets support and gives support. The first sentence gives support but gets none. The next two sentences don't argue for it; they build on it. With no support coming in, it is a premise.

The scholar doesn't attack this view. The scholar builds on it. If the argument were designed to discredit the idea that laws deter by threatening punishment, we'd see reasons against it. Instead, the rest of the argument depends on it being true.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
old_steps.body: A successful legal system prohibits only those few behaviors that citizens find absolute intolerable.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: The purpose of laws in a legal system is to deter bad actions by threatening punishment if you perform them, but this only works if people think they're likely to get punished for committing those actions, and the more behaviors that are criminalized, the less likely someone will be caught and punished.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: When we read Role and Main Conclusion we anticipate the conclusion being "hidden" by appearing as the First Sentence or as some Rebuttal / Pivot moment. But this first sentence is not supported, so it can't be a conclusion. And the pivot sentence prefaced by "But" is also not supported, so it can't be a conclusion. Meanwhile, we have a very conspicuous conclusion indicator on the last sentence (we know any time we see so, thus, hence, therefore that it will be a conclusion, even if it's not the main one). But in this case, it's the main conclusion, because the other three ideas combine to get us there. Why do successful legal systems want to limit the number of criminalized actions to the most intolerable ones? Because laws only work as a threat if people think they're likely to be caught and punished, and the more actions we criminalize the less likely people are to be caught / punished.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: We're being asked about the Role of the first claim. We'd say it's part of the Support for the conclusion in the final sentence.

old_notes.body: This answer says the statement supports an implicit conclusion about a "significant police force." The argument never mentions police, enforcement resources, or staffing. The argument's actual conclusion is that a successful legal system prohibits only a few intolerable behaviors. While one might extrapolate that effective enforcement requires resources, that inference is not made in this argument. The statement about deterrence supports the explicit conclusion about limiting prohibitions, not an unstated conclusion about police staffing.

The conclusion of the argument is that a successful legal system prohibits only a few behaviors that citizens find absolutely intolerable. The statement in question — that law's purpose is deterrence through punishment — is not this conclusion. It is the starting premise from which the argument builds. The conclusion is introduced by "therefore" at the end of the argument. The deterrence statement appears at the very beginning and provides the foundational definition of law's purpose. The argument uses this definition, combines it with additional premises about belief and probability, and arrives at the conclusion about limiting prohibitions. The statement is a building block, not the destination.

The statement that "the purpose of a law is to deter certain actions by threatening to punish those performing the actions" is a premise of the argument. It is the first claim in a chain of reasoning that leads to the conclusion. The argument does not derive this statement from other claims — it is asserted as a foundational principle. From this premise, the argument builds: deterrence requires belief in likely punishment, that belief erodes as prohibitions multiply, therefore successful systems must limit their prohibitions. The deterrence statement is not the conclusion (which appears after "therefore"), not an intermediate conclusion (it is not derived from other premises), and not a view being challenged (the scholar endorses it as the foundation of the argument).

An intermediate conclusion is a claim that is both derived from premises AND used to support a further conclusion — it serves as both a conclusion of earlier reasoning and a premise for later reasoning. The deterrence statement is not derived from any other claims in the argument. It is simply asserted as a starting point. No prior reasoning leads to it; it is the first claim made. Because it has no premises supporting it within the argument, it cannot be an intermediate conclusion. It is a straightforward premise — a building block offered without prior justification.

This answer says the statement is a view the argument is designed to discredit. But the scholar endorses this statement — it is the foundation of the argument, not the target of it. The scholar uses the deterrence definition of law to build toward the conclusion about limiting prohibitions. If the scholar were trying to discredit the deterrence view, the argument would need to present evidence or reasoning against it. Instead, the argument accepts the deterrence view and draws implications from it. The argument works with the statement, not against it.

steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
steps.body: There's unlikely to be a widespread, grassroots effort for new, more restrictive air pollution controls at this time.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: People generally notice and are concerned about only the most obvious public health problems. And most people are currently well aware that contaminated water is a much more widespread threat to the community than is air pollution (such as ozone).

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion and Role, the conclusion is usually found earlier than the support, but in this case it was the final sentence, signified by "Hence". Because this is Role, we want to be highly alert for whether that "Hence" is actually just an Intermediate Conclusion, but in this case we can tell it's the main conclusion because the 1st and 3rd claim combine to support this 4th claim. There are four claims in this argument, and structurally they go in this order:
    1. Premise
    2. Counterpoint (although)
    3. Premise
    4. Conclusion (hence)
    We're being asked about the first sentence, which was one of the two premises for the conclusion in the final sentence.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The stem asks about the first sentence, one of the two premises. Predict: a premise that supports the conclusion that a widespread grassroots push for stricter air pollution controls is unlikely right now.

notes.body: A aims the first sentence at the wrong claim. The water claim isn't argued for. It is reported as something most people already know. The first sentence teams up with it instead: people care only about the most obvious problems, and right now the obvious one is water, so no grassroots push on air pollution. It supports the conclusion, not the water claim.

B names the target and the destination. The first sentence is a general rule about attention, and the argument applies it: people care only about the most obvious health problems, water is the problem people are aware of, so air pollution won't draw a grassroots effort now. The first sentence is a premise for the "Hence" claim.

The move to repeat: when an argument pairs a general rule with a specific fact, the rule is usually a premise the conclusion applies. Check where the rule is aimed, and match the answer to that claim.

C says the first sentence explains why people are aware of the water problem. The argument never asks why. It states the awareness as a fact and uses it. The first sentence is about what people pay attention to, and the argument aims it at the conclusion about air pollution controls.

The "indisputable evidence" belongs to the ozone claim in the second sentence, about danger to severe asthmatics. The first sentence is about what people notice, not about whether ozone is dangerous. It offers no evidence about ozone at all.

The main conclusion follows "Hence": a widespread grassroots effort for stricter air pollution controls is unlikely now. Ask why we should believe that. Partly because people notice only the most obvious problems. The first sentence answers the why, so it is support, not the conclusion.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for something like "it was a premise / evidence / partial support for the Conclusion that there's unlikely to be a widespread effort for more air pollution controls right now".

old_notes.body: This answer says the targeted statement supports the claim that contaminated water is a widespread threat. But the argument does not use the "people notice only obvious problems" principle to argue that water contamination is a serious threat — the argument treats the seriousness of water contamination as an independent fact that most people already know. The targeted statement instead combines with the water contamination fact to support the main conclusion: people will not mobilize for stricter air pollution controls. The relationship is: because people focus on the most obvious threats (targeted statement), and because water contamination is currently the obvious threat (separate premise), people will not push for air controls (conclusion). The targeted statement supports the conclusion about inaction, not the premise about water.

The targeted statement — that people generally notice and are concerned about only the most obvious public health problems — functions as a premise supporting the main conclusion that there is unlikely to be a widespread, grassroots effort for stricter air pollution controls. The argument's logic is: people focus on the most obvious threats (this premise) + water contamination is currently the obvious threat in the community (another premise) + ozone pollution is a less visible concern (implicit) = people will not rally for stricter ozone controls (conclusion). The targeted statement provides the behavioral principle that connects the specific factual observations to the predicted public response. Without this premise, the facts about ozone danger and water contamination prominence would not lead to the conclusion about grassroots inaction.

This answer, like (A), misidentifies the inferential target. It claims the targeted statement explains why people are currently aware of water contamination's severity. But the argument does not use the "people focus on obvious problems" principle to explain awareness of water contamination. Public awareness of water contamination is treated as an independent fact, not as something that needs to be explained by the targeted statement. The targeted statement and the water awareness fact are parallel premises that jointly support the main conclusion. Additionally, "explaining" awareness of water contamination would require the targeted statement to show why water contamination is obvious, but the statement is about what people attend to, not about what makes a problem obvious. The causal direction proposed by this answer does not match the argument's actual structure.

The targeted statement is not presented as evidence for ozone's danger. The argument treats ozone's danger as a separate factual premise supported by "indisputable evidence" — that language attaches to the ozone claim, not to the targeted statement about public attention. The targeted statement is a behavioral generalization about what people notice and care about; it has nothing to do with establishing the medical or environmental danger of ozone. These are completely different types of claims serving different functions in the argument. The ozone danger premise establishes the underlying public health reality; the targeted statement explains why people are unlikely to act on that reality. Different roles, different parts of the argument.

The targeted statement is not the main conclusion — the main conclusion is the prediction that there is unlikely to be a widespread grassroots effort for stricter air pollution controls. The targeted statement is a general principle about human behavior that supports this specific prediction. The test for identifying the main conclusion is: what claim does everything else in the argument work to support? The targeted statement works to support the prediction about grassroots inaction; the prediction does not work to support the targeted statement. Additionally, the targeted statement is presented as a general given — a behavioral observation — while the main conclusion is a specific prediction derived from applying that general observation to particular circumstances.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Our mastery of Latin and Ancient Greek is at best imperfect.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The best students of a modern language can immerse themselves in a country where that language is spoken in order to attain nearly perfect knowledge. But you can't travel back in time (to ancient Greece) to spend a year at Plato's Academy (immersing yourself in the ancient Greek language).

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Role and Main Conclusion, the conclusion very often sits in the first sentence or right after a pivot. So hear the first sentence as a possible opinion: our mastery of Latin and Ancient Greek is "at best imperfect." If the rest of the passage supports it, it's the main conclusion.

It does. The second sentence sets up a contrast. On one side, the best students of a modern language can immerse themselves where it is spoken and get close to perfect knowledge. On the other side, you can't spend a year abroad at Plato's Academy. Immersion is open for living languages and closed for ancient ones. That contrast is why the classicist thinks mastery of the ancient languages falls short.

Notice what the Plato's Academy line is. It isn't a general statement that ancient immersion is impossible. It is one vivid case that makes the point.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The target claim is the second half of the contrast, given as a concrete case. Predict: support for the first sentence, possibly described as an example or as one side of a comparison.

notes.body: The main conclusion is the first sentence: our mastery of the ancient languages is imperfect. Ask why we should believe it, and the Plato's Academy line is part of the answer. A claim that answers the why for another claim is support, not the main conclusion.

B describes the claim's job piece by piece. There is "a contrast": modern-language students can immerse themselves, and students of ancient languages can't. The claim points it up "by example": the Plato's Academy line makes the second side concrete with one trip nobody can take. And it is a contrast "from which the conclusion is drawn": imperfect mastery follows from it.

The move to repeat: abstract role answers are easiest to check in pieces. Match each phrase to a specific part of the passage, and reject the answer if any piece has nothing to land on.

C says the claim has "no logical relation" to the conclusion. Remove it and see. The second sentence would describe only what modern-language students can do, with nothing to compare against. The contrast that supports the conclusion would disappear, so the claim is doing logical work.

D starts well, because the claim is support. The problem is "guarantees the truth". Even granting that you can't visit Plato's Academy, the conclusion needs more: that immersion, or something like it, is needed for nearly perfect knowledge. The modern-language sentence only says the best students may get there through immersion. The claim helps the conclusion. It doesn't force it.

An ancillary conclusion would be a claim the argument supports on its way to the main point. Nothing in the passage argues that you can't travel back in time. It is offered as plain fact. A claim with nothing supporting it can't be a conclusion of any kind.

old_steps.body: Our mastery of Latin and Ancient Greek is at best imperfect.

old_steps.label: Evidence

But you can't travel back in time (to ancient Greece) to spend a year at Plato's Academy (immersing yourself in the ancient Greek language).

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: Whenever we read Role and Main Conclusion arguments, we remind ourselves that 90% of the time the conclusion is: the First Sentence, or some Rebuttal / Pivot idea. That helps us hear the first sentence as an Author Opinion, right out of the gate ("at best imperfect"). If she goes on to support that idea, we know it's the main conclusion. She does indeed. The final two claims combine to show why our mastery of ancient Latin and Greek isn't the best: best requires immersion, and you can't do immersion with ancient Latin and Greek.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: We're being asked about the 3rd claim, which was one of the two premises. So let's look for something like "Support, Evidence, Premise" for the conclusion in the 1st sentence.

old_notes.body: The main conclusion of the argument is that our mastery of Latin and Ancient Greek is at best imperfect — the first sentence of the passage. The Plato's Academy statement is not the main conclusion; it is part of the supporting reasoning. It serves as an example illustrating why mastery of dead languages cannot match that of living ones. On Role of Statement questions, the main conclusion is the claim that everything else supports. Here, the imperfect-mastery claim is what the Plato's Academy example ultimately helps to prove. The example provides support; the conclusion receives it.

The Plato's Academy statement serves as a concrete example that highlights the critical contrast between modern and ancient language learning. The argument's reasoning depends on a contrast: modern language students can achieve near-perfect mastery through immersion in a country where the language is spoken, but no comparable immersion is possible for dead languages. The statement that you cannot visit Plato's Academy crystallizes this contrast through a specific, memorable image. It is not an independent premise that directly proves the conclusion on its own; rather, it illustrates by example the broader point about the impossibility of ancient-language immersion, and the conclusion (imperfect mastery) is drawn from this contrast. "Points up by example a contrast from which the conclusion is drawn" precisely captures this structural role.

The Plato's Academy statement is far from a mere rhetorical flourish with no logical relation to the conclusion. It plays a specific structural role: it illustrates the impossibility of immersion in dead languages, which is the core of the argument's reasoning. Without this contrast between what modern-language students can do and what ancient-language students cannot, the conclusion about imperfect mastery would have no support. The statement is logically integral to the argument — it makes the abstract reasoning concrete and provides the evidential basis for the conclusion. Dismissing it as decoration ignores its essential function in the argument's logical structure.

The statement does not "guarantee" the truth of the conclusion. A premise that guarantees a conclusion would make the argument deductively valid on its own. But the Plato's Academy reference alone does not prove that mastery of ancient languages is imperfect — it requires the additional reasoning about immersion being the pathway to near-perfect mastery. The statement is one piece of the argument, not a logically sufficient condition for the conclusion. Furthermore, calling it a "premise" overstates its independence: it functions more as an illustrative example of a broader contrast than as a standalone premise. "Guarantees the truth" is far too strong a characterization of its role.

An ancillary conclusion is a subsidiary claim that the argument establishes along the way to its main conclusion — an intermediate conclusion. The Plato's Academy statement is not something the argument is trying to prove. It is presented as an obvious fact that everyone would accept: of course you cannot travel back in time. The argument uses this fact as evidence; it does not derive it from other evidence. A conclusion (main or ancillary) is supported by other claims in the argument. This statement is not supported by anything — it supports other claims. That makes it part of the evidence, not a conclusion of any kind.
